children.title: What this server costs, measured
children.lead: Every number on this page was measured on 2026-11-01, on the image built from commit 647b8b7, on one shared Linux machine: the server held to two cores and the chart’s 768 MiB, PostgreSQL, the load and the synthetic shoppers on cores of their own. Nothing here is estimated; how to measure it again is at the end.

points.name: With the AOT cache
points.text: Ready to serve 1,006 ms after docker run, the median of 11 starts; the first home page at 1,133 ms.

points.name: Without it
points.text: 1,713 ms to ready and 1,929 ms to the first home page: the same image, its cache switched off.

points.name: What the cache buys
points.text: 710 ms (± 109 ms) to ready — 41 % of the start without it — and 811 ms (± 112 ms) to the first home page.

points.name: Docker’s own share
points.text: 160 ms of each start is docker run itself.

points.name: Verdict
points.text: Green: distinguishable, past the lines set before the first run, and every start with the cache used it.

points.name: The load
points.text: 100 anonymous requests a second for 6 rounds of 60 s, the five routes below in turn, beside the synthetic shoppers walking the whole path.

points.name: The home page
points.text: 18.7 ms at the median, 94.4 ms at p99.

points.name: A category
points.text: 7.3 ms at the median, 53.4 ms at p99.

points.name: A product
points.text: 7.7 ms at the median, 62.9 ms at p99.

points.name: Search suggestions
points.text: 18.3 ms at the median, 97.3 ms at p99.

points.name: Live orders
points.text: 7.1 ms at the median, 55.7 ms at p99.

points.name: At twice the rate
points.text: 200 a second, the same morning, while other work loaded the machine: the first four rounds held p99 under 184 ms, then the server fell behind — 93 % of the requests answered, p99 up to 5,170 ms.

points.name: Verdict
points.text: Grey at 100 a second: every route inside its lines, but from the fourth round on the shoppers’ checkouts failed — the store’s delivery windows were full — so the load beside the requests was no longer theirs; red at 200, on the loaded machine.

points.name: The server
points.text: 3.4 ms of CPU per request of that mix (± 0.6), over what the shoppers alone cost; 4.4 ms (± 2.1) in the run at 200 a second.

points.name: PostgreSQL
points.text: 4.6 ms more per request, in the database’s own container.

points.name: Verdict
points.text: Green at 100 a second; grey at 200, its interval wider.

points.name: At its peak
points.text: 685 MiB of the 768 MiB limit (89 %), as the container counts it, with the JVM’s heap sized from the limit; its resident set, shared files included, at most 686 MiB.

points.name: Under a smaller limit
points.text: Killed — the JVM out of heap — under 128 MiB with the same load; it lived under 192 MiB.

points.name: Verdict
points.text: Grey: never killed and never restarted, but past the headroom set before the first run.

points.name: Pre-registered
points.text: The questions, the lines a verdict is read against and the rules that stop a run were frozen before the first number; a check fails if a byte of them moves.

points.name: Interleaved
points.text: The start-up arms took turns in every round and the first round was thrown away; a second arm with the cache is the ruler, and a start delayed by one second the control the harness must see.

points.name: Open-loop
points.text: k6 offered requests at a fixed rate whatever the server answered, from cores the server did not have; CPU and memory are the container’s own counters, not the machine’s.

points.name: Again
points.text: scripts/measure-stack.py — startup, then load — on Linux with Docker and k6; summarise turns the raw runs into this page’s data, and the check holds the page to them.
